But now I am instead like an angel who has been demoted and banished down to the lower world, deprived of joy by you for no reason at all. …… By my nature I too was benevolent and kind; it was all suffering that made me turn into a demon.","slots":{"creature":{"rendering":"","gloss":"","sense":"not in quote"},"adam":{"rendering":"亚当","gloss":"Adam (transliterated name)","sense":"Adam, named"},"fallen_angel":{"rendering":"像一个被贬谪下界的天使","gloss":"like one (passive) demoted-banished down-to-lower-world angel","sense":"fallen angel"},"drivest":{"rendering":"被你剥夺了快乐","gloss":"(passive) by you stripped-away (perfective) joy","sense":"deprived / excluded"},"misdeed":{"rendering":"无缘无故","gloss":"without cause, without reason","sense":"other"},"benevolent":{"rendering":"仁慈","gloss":"humane-merciful","sense":"benevolent / well-wishing"},"misery":{"rendering":"痛苦","gloss":"pain-bitterness","sense":"suffering / pain"},"fiend":{"rendering":"恶魔","gloss":"evil demon","sense":"devil / demon"},"virtuous":{"rendering":"","gloss":"","sense":"not in quote"}},"connotations":[{"word":"贬谪下界","kind":"folkloric","note":"贬谪 is the vocabulary of an official's punitive demotion to a distant post, and 下界 evokes Chinese tales of immortals banished from heaven to the mortal world, such as Zhu Bajie in Journey to the West. This recasts Milton's rebellious fall as a heavenly bureaucracy's exile of an offender.","check":true},{"word":"无缘无故","kind":"register / tone","note":"This is a colloquial set phrase, 'for no reason whatsoever'. It replaces Shelley's claim of innocence ('for no misdeed', implying no wrong was committed) with a complaint that the act was arbitrary, so the moral and legal sense of 'misdeed' is lost.","check":false},{"word":"本性也是仁慈、善良的","kind":"moral","note":"本性 (innate nature) together with 仁慈 (with its Confucian 仁) can recall the Mencian doctrine that human nature is originally good. The plea thus becomes a claim about innate goodness rather than a past condition ('I was').","check":true},{"word":"都是痛苦让我变成了恶魔","kind":"grammatical","note":"都是 ('it is all…') puts the blame wholly on suffering, and 变成 ('turned into') makes the demon a transformation rather than an identity. This intensifies the self-exculpation.","check":false},{"word":"啊","kind":"register / tone","note":"The sentence-final particle 啊 adds an oral, plaintive exclamation absent from Shelley's measured 'I ought to be thy Adam'.","check":false}],"demonic_pitiable":1,"biblical_secular":1,"scales_reason":"Innate goodness (本性), total blame placed on suffering (都是), the hedging simile 像 and the plaintive 啊 make the creature more pitiable, and recasting the Miltonic fall as Chinese celestial banishment (贬谪下界) softens the biblical frame, although 亚当, 天使 and 恶魔 keep it partly in place."}
message.reasoning:
I'm translating the quote back and checking which words belong inside versus outside the quotation marks—"creature" falls outside, so now I need to verify where "Adam" and the rest of the phrases fall relative to the quoted text.

"Fallen angel" captures 贬谪下界的天使 reasonably, though it carries Chinese banished-immortal connotations (like 谪仙 or Zhu Bajie's demotion) rather than the Miltonic rebellion sense. "无缘无故" (without cause) drops the "misdeed" framing entirely, reading more like a flat denial of reason than an admission of innocence, so I'm marking it as "other" rather than mapping it cleanly. "仁慈" works fine for "benevolent," carrying a mild Confucian 仁 resonance, while 痛苦 and 恶魔 map straightforwardly onto "misery" and "fiend." "Virtuous" doesn't appear in the quoted text at all.

Weighing the overall tone, I'd put demonic_pitiable around 1, since the plaintive particles and emphasis on innate goodness push it slightly toward sympathetic framing, and biblical_secular also around 1, since the Chinese cosmological imagery softens the Miltonic religious register without erasing it entirely.
